subject: math
title: Pictographs: Read, Make from a Tally, Compare and Find the Total
seo_title: Grade 2 Pictographs Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Pictorial representation of concrete graphs, using one-to-one correspondence
meta_desc: Free Grade 2 math worksheets on pictographs where 1 picture = 1: read rows, make a pictograph from a tally, find the most, the fewest and how many more, add totals and draw conclusions. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the BC curriculum.
key_big: One picture stands for one. Count the pictures in a row to read it.
key_sub: Touch each picture once and follow the right row. A tally group of 5 is 5, not 4. How many more means take away; how many in all means add every row.
body_html:
One picture for each

A pictograph uses pictures to show data. In Grade 2, 1 picture = 1. One star can stand for one student, one day or one bird. The key tells you what one picture means. The pictures are all the same size and line up, so the rows are easy to compare.

Example

How many students chose lacrosse?

Touch each star in the Lacrosse row once: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Answer: 6 students

Make a pictograph from a tally

Read each tally first. A group of 5 has four lines and one line across. Then draw one picture for each tally mark, in the same row.

Most, fewest and how many more

The longest row has the most. The shortest row has the fewest. To find how many more, take the smaller number away from the bigger number.

Example

In the sport pictograph, how many more students chose soccer than skiing?

Soccer 7, skiing 3. 7 − 3 = 4.

Answer: 4 more students

Find the total

To find how many in all, add the numbers in every row. To find how many did not choose something, add all the other rows.

Example

How many students voted in the sport pictograph?

7 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 20.

Answer: 20 students

Ask a question, then explain

Start with a question, such as “What is your favourite sport?” Collect the answers with tally marks, make the pictograph, and then say what it tells you. A pictograph of one class tells you about that class, not about every student in BC.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting one picture twice or skipping oneTouch each picture once as you count
Reading the row above or belowPut your finger on the label and follow the row
Counting a group of 5 tally marks as 4The line across is the 5th mark
Adding when the question says how many moreHow many more means take away
Looking at how long a row is when pictures are different sizesCount the pictures
Giving the number of rows as the totalAdd the pictures in every row

faq.q: What do Grade 2 students learn about pictographs in BC math?
faq.a: In the BC curriculum, Grade 2 students show data in concrete graphs and pictographs using one-to-one correspondence, so each picture stands for one thing. They read the graph, compare rows, find totals and explain what the data tells them.

faq.q: What does one-to-one correspondence mean in a pictograph?
faq.a: It means one picture stands for one thing, such as one star for one student. To read the graph, count the pictures in a row.

faq.q: How do you make a pictograph from a tally chart?
faq.a: Count each tally (a group of 5 has a line across), then draw one picture for each mark in that row. Make all the pictures the same size, line them up, and add a title and a key.

faq.q: How can I practise pictographs with my child at home?
faq.a: Ask family members a question, such as their favourite fruit, and tally the answers. Then draw one sticker or picture for each answer and ask which has the most and how many more.

items.e: Each star = 1 student. Touch each star in the Orca row and count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. So 6 students. (4 is the Bald eagle row.)
Count the stars in the Salmon row, one at a time: 7 stars. So 7 students. (5 is the Black bear row.)
The Bald eagle row has 4 stars. Each star = 1 student, so 4 students. (6 is the Orca row above it.)
Count each row: orca 6, bald eagle 4, salmon 7, black bear 5. Black bear has 5 stars.
Look at the key: one star = 1 student. Each student who voted got one star.

items.q: How many days were rainy?
items.e: Each square = 1 day. Count the squares in the Rain row: 7. So 7 rainy days. (4 is the Cloudy row.)

items.q: How many days were sunny?
items.e: The Sunny row has 2 squares, so 2 days were sunny. (4 is the Cloudy row above it.)

items.q: Which weather happened on 4 days?
items.e: Count each row: rain 7, cloudy 4, sunny 2, snow 1. Cloudy has 4 squares.

items.q: How many days had snow?
items.e: The Snow row has only 1 square, so it snowed on 1 day. (2 is the Sunny row.)

items.q: How many juncos came to the feeder?
items.e: Each circle = 1 bird. Count the Junco row: 6 circles. So 6 juncos. (3 is the Steller’s jay row above it.)

items.q: How many Steller’s jays came to the feeder?
items.e: The Steller’s jay row has 3 circles, so 3 Steller’s jays came. (8 is the Chickadee row.)

items.q: Which bird came 8 times?
items.e: Count each row: chickadee 8, Steller’s jay 3, junco 6, robin 5. The Chickadee row has 8 circles.

items.q: How many robins came to the feeder?
items.e: Count the circles in the Robin row: 5. (6 is the Junco row above it.)

items.q: How many students chose blueberries?
items.e: Each square = 1 student. Count the Blueberries row: 10 squares. So 10 students. (5 is the Cherries row above it.)

items.q: How many students chose apples?
items.e: The Apples row has 9 squares, so 9 students chose apples. (5 is the Cherries row.)

items.q: Which fruit has 4 squares?
items.e: Count each row: apples 9, cherries 5, blueberries 10, peaches 4. Peaches has 4 squares.

items.q: Which fruit has 1 more square than apples?
items.e: Apples has 9 squares. 9 + 1 = 10. Blueberries has 10 squares.

items.q: A pictograph has 6 stars in the Soccer row. Each star = 1 student. How many students chose soccer?
items.e: One star stands for one student. 6 stars means 6 students.
The salmon has 7 stars. 7 − 1 = 6. The Orca row has 6 stars.

items.q: Leah counts the Junco row and gets 7. What went wrong?
items.e: The Junco row has 6 circles. 7 is 1 too many, so she counted one circle twice. Touch each circle once as you count.

sets.title: Make a pictograph from a tally

items.q: How many circles go in the Walk row?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 3 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8. So it is 8. Each circle = 1 student, so draw 8 circles.

items.q: How many circles go in the Bus row?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, then 6. So it is 6. Each circle = 1 student, so draw 6 circles.

items.q: How many circles go in the Car row?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5. Count 5. So it is 5. Each circle = 1 student, so draw 5 circles.

items.q: How many circles go in the Bike row?
items.e: Read the tally: 3 single marks. So it is 3. Each circle = 1 student, so draw 3 circles.

items.q: How many stars go in the Aquarium row?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So it is 9. Each star = 1 student, so draw 9 stars.

items.q: How many stars go in the Stanley Park row?
items.e: Read the tally: 2 groups of 5. Count 5, 10. So it is 10. Each star = 1 student, so draw 10 stars.

items.q: How many stars go in the Science centre row?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, then 6, 7. So it is 7. Each star = 1 student, so draw 7 stars.

items.q: Each circle = 1. Which row matches the tally?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, then 6, 7. So it is 7. Row B has 7 circles. (Counting the group of 5 as 4 gives 6.)
Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So it is 9. Row D has 9 circles. (Counting the group of 5 as 4 gives 8.)

items.q: Each circle = 1. Which row matches the tally?
items.e: Read the tally: 1 group of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, then 6. So it is 6. Row A has 6 circles. (Counting the group of 5 as 4 gives 5.)

items.q: Which row of the pictograph does not match the tally?
items.e: Check every row: count the tally, then count the pictures. The Cheese tally is 1 group of 5 and 4 more: 9. The Cheese row has only 8 circles. The group of 5 was counted as 4.

items.q: Which row of the pictograph does not match the tally?
items.e: Check every row: count the tally, then count the pictures. The Fish tally has 4 marks, but the Fish row has 5 squares. One extra square was drawn.
Check every row: count the tally, then count the pictures. The Red tally is 1 group of 5: 5. The Red row has only 4 stars. The group of 5 was counted as 4.

items.q: The tally for Soccer shows 2 groups of 5 and 3 more. Each ball = 1 student. How many balls go in the Soccer row?
items.e: Count by 5s for the groups: 5, 10. Then 11, 12, 13. Draw 13 balls. (11 counts each group as 4. 5 adds 2 + 3.)

items.q: Every picture in a pictograph should …
c: be the same size and line up
items.e: In a Grade 2 pictograph, 1 picture = 1. All pictures are the same size and line up, so you can compare the rows.

items.q: Why does a pictograph need a key?
items.e: The key shows one picture and what it stands for, such as “= 1 student.”

items.q: Ji-woo’s tally says 12 students chose hockey. Each star = 1 student. How many stars go in the Hockey row?
items.e: 1 star for each student: 12 students need 12 stars. (4 stars draws one star for each group of 5 and one for each extra mark.)

items.q: Each picture = 1. How many pictures show this tally?
items.e: Read the tally: 2 groups of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, 10, then 11. So it is 11. Draw 11 pictures. (9 counts each group as 4. 3 adds 2 + 1.)

items.q: Each picture = 1. How many pictures show this tally?
items.e: Read the tally: 2 groups of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, 10, then 11, 12, 13, 14. So it is 14. Draw 14 pictures. (12 counts each group as 4. 6 adds 2 + 4.)

items.q: A pictograph row has 6 squares. What should the tally for this row show?
items.e: 6 = 5 + 1. Make one group of 5 (the fifth mark goes across), then 1 more mark.

sets.title: Most, fewest and how many more

items.e: The stars line up, so the longest row has the most. Swimming has 9 stars.
The shortest row has the fewest. Lacrosse has 4 stars.
Swimming 9, lacrosse 4. How many more means take away: 9 − 4 = 5. (13 adds them.)
Soccer 8, hockey 6. 8 − 6 = 2. (14 adds them. 4 compares soccer with lacrosse, the wrong row.)
Soccer 8, lacrosse 4. How many fewer means take away: 8 − 4 = 4. (12 adds them.)

items.q: On which day did the class see the most salmon?
items.e: The longest row has the most. Wednesday has 10 circles.

items.q: On which day did the class see the fewest salmon?
items.e: The shortest row has the fewest. Monday has 3 circles.

items.q: How many more salmon did they see on Wednesday than on Thursday?
items.e: Wednesday 10, Thursday 5. 10 − 5 = 5. (15 adds them. 3 compares Wednesday with Tuesday, the wrong row.)

items.q: How many more salmon did they see on Tuesday than on Monday?
items.e: Tuesday 7, Monday 3. 7 − 3 = 4. (10 adds them.)

items.q: On which day did they see 1 more salmon than on Thursday?
items.e: Thursday has 5 circles. 5 + 1 = 6. Friday has 6 circles.

items.q: Which sport got more votes?
items.e: Count, do not look at the length. Soccer has 5 circles and hockey has 7. The Soccer row looks longer only because its circles are big and far apart.

items.q: How many more votes did hockey get than soccer?
items.e: Hockey 7, soccer 5. 7 − 5 = 2. (12 adds them.)

items.q: Which two activities got the same number of votes?
items.e: Count each row: skiing 7, swimming 5, camping 7, biking 3. Skiing and camping both have 7.

items.q: Which activity did the fewest students choose?
items.e: The shortest row has the fewest. Biking has 3 squares.

items.q: How many more students chose skiing than biking?
items.e: Skiing 7, biking 3. 7 − 3 = 4. (10 adds them. 2 compares swimming with biking, the wrong row.)

items.q: How many more students need to choose biking so it ties with swimming?
items.e: Swimming has 5. Biking has 3. 3 + 2 = 5, so 2 more students. (8 adds 5 + 3.)

items.q: In a pictograph, the Orca row has 9 stars and the Black bear row has 6 stars. Which is true?
items.e: 9 − 6 = 3. Orca has the longer row, so orca has 3 more. (15 adds them.)
Soccer has 8. 8 − 2 = 6. Hockey has 6 stars.

items.q: On which days did they see more than 5 salmon?
items.e: More than 5 means 6 or more. Tuesday 7, Wednesday 10 and Friday 6. Thursday has exactly 5, which is not more than 5, so it is not “Tuesday to Friday.”
Swimming 9, soccer 8, hockey 6, lacrosse 4. Most to fewest: 9, 8, 6, 4.

items.q: How many pets does the pictograph show in all?
items.e: Add every row: 9 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 21. (4 is the number of rows, not pets.)

items.q: How many dogs and cats are there altogether?
items.e: Dogs 9, cats 6. Altogether means add: 9 + 6 = 15. (3 takes away. 13 adds the Fish row by mistake.)

items.q: How many pets are not dogs?
items.e: Add the other rows: 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. (21 is all the pets. 10 forgets the Rabbit row.)

items.q: How many fish and rabbits are there altogether?
items.e: Fish 4, rabbits 2. 4 + 2 = 6. (2 takes away. 10 uses the Cat row instead of the Rabbit row.)

items.q: How many days does the pictograph show in all?
items.e: Add every row: 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 30. November has 30 days, so this checks out.

items.q: How many days had rain or fog?
items.e: Rain 12, fog 3. 12 + 3 = 15. (9 takes away. 21 adds the Cloudy row instead of the Fog row.)

items.q: How many days did not have rain?
items.e: Add the other rows: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18. Or 30 − 12 = 18. (12 is the rainy days.)

items.q: How many days were rainy or cloudy?
items.e: Rain 12, cloudy 9. 12 + 9 = 21. (3 takes away. 18 adds the Sunny row instead of the Cloudy row.)

items.q: How many books did the four friends read in all?
items.e: Add every row: 8 + 5 + 11 + 7 = 31. (4 is the number of friends. 11 is only Chloe.)

items.q: How many books did Simran and Chloe read together?
items.e: Simran 8, Chloe 11. 8 + 11 = 19. (3 takes away. 13 adds Arjun’s row instead of Chloe’s.)

items.q: How many books did Arjun and Noah read together?
items.e: Arjun 5, Noah 7. 5 + 7 = 12. (2 takes away. 13 adds Simran’s row instead of Noah’s.)

items.q: The four friends want to read 40 books. How many more books do they need?
items.e: They read 31. Count up from 31 to 40: 9. So 40 − 31 = 9 more books. (71 adds 40 + 31.)

items.q: How many cans did the class collect in all?
items.e: Add every row: 8 + 11 + 9 = 28. (3 is the number of weeks. 11 is only week 2.)

items.q: How many cans did they collect in week 1 and week 2?
items.e: Week 1: 8. Week 2: 11. 8 + 11 = 19. (17 adds week 3 instead of week 2.)

items.q: The class wants 40 cans. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: They have 28. Count up: 28 to 30 is 2, then 30 to 40 is 10. 2 + 10 = 12 cans. (68 adds. 2 stops counting at 30.)

items.q: How many cats and rabbits are there altogether?
items.e: Cats 6, rabbits 2. 6 + 2 = 8. (4 takes away. 10 adds the Fish row instead of the Rabbit row.)

items.q: 3 more students say they have a fish. How many pets will the pictograph show now?
items.e: There are 21 pets now. 3 more: 21 + 3 = 24. (7 is the new Fish row only.)

items.q: Kai’s pictograph has 3 rows. They have 10, 10 and 6 stars. How many stars are there in all?
items.e: Count by 10s, then on: 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26. So 26 stars. (16 adds only one 10.)

items.q: A pictograph has 14 stars in the Hockey row and 23 stars in the Soccer row. How many stars altogether?
items.e: Add tens, then ones: 10 + 20 = 30 and 4 + 3 = 7. 30 + 7 = 37. (9 takes away. 47 adds one ten too many.)

items.q: There are 25 students in the class. The class pictograph has 22 pictures. Each picture = 1 student. How many students have not voted yet?
What question did the class ask?
c: How do you get to school?
items.e: The rows are ways to get to school: walk, bus, car and bike. Each student answered “How do you get to school?”

items.q: Which sentence is true?
c: More students walk than come by car.
items.e: Walk 9 and car 7: 9 is more than 7, so this is true. Walk has the most, not bike. Car has 3 more than bus (7 − 4), not the other way.

items.q: Arjun says, “Most students in BC walk to school.” Is he right?
c: No. The data is from one class.
No. Bus has the longest row.
Yes. Walk has the longest row.
items.e: The source says the data is from Ms. Gill’s class. It tells us about this class only, not every student in BC.

items.q: The class did this survey in June. Why might fewer students bike in January?
c: It is cold, wet and dark.
items.e: In January it is cold and rainy, and it gets dark early, so fewer students bike. When we explain data, we think about when it was collected.

items.q: 3 students who come by car start to walk. How many students will walk?
items.e: 9 students walk now. 3 more will walk: 9 + 3 = 12. (6 takes away. 4 is how many will still come by car. 16 adds all 7 car students.)

items.q: How many students answered the survey?
items.e: Each student gave one answer. Add every row: 9 + 4 + 7 + 3 = 23. (4 is the number of rows.)
Tug-of-war has the longest row: 10 students. More students chose it than any other activity.
Add the other rows: 6 + 5 + 8 = 19. (29 is everyone. 13 forgets the Sack race row.)
Obstacle course now has 8 + 3 = 11 votes. 11 is more than 10 (tug-of-war).
Relay race 5, tug-of-war 10. 5 + 5 = 10, so 5 is half of 10. She is right.

items.q: Mei wants to find out the favourite fruit of her class. Which question should she ask?
items.e: Her question must ask each student for their favourite fruit. “Do you like apples?” only tells her about apples.

items.q: Ethan wants to know which birds visit the school feeder. What is the best way to collect the data?
items.e: He can find out by watching. He makes one tally mark for each bird he sees at the feeder. A favourite bird is not the same as a bird that comes to the feeder.

items.q: Nadia asks her class, “Have you seen an orca?” Which rows should her pictograph have?
items.e: Each student can only answer yes or no, so her pictograph needs a Yes row and a No row.

items.q: Lucas asked 24 students. His pictograph has 22 stars. Each star = 1 student. What went wrong?
items.e: 24 students need 24 stars. 24 − 22 = 2, so 2 stars are missing. Check each tally mark again.

items.q: A class will make a pictograph of favourite snacks. What must it have?
c: A title, labels and a key
A different picture for each child
items.e: A title tells what the graph is about, the labels name the rows, and the key tells what 1 picture means.

items.q: At the Terry Fox Run, Owen ran 6 laps, Zara ran 9 laps and Ryan ran 4 laps. How many more laps did Zara run than Ryan?
items.e: Zara 9, Ryan 4. 9 − 4 = 5. (13 adds them. 3 compares Zara with Owen, the wrong person.)

items.q: For the food bank, Hana’s school collected 18 cans in week 1, 24 cans in week 2 and 31 cans in week 3. How many cans did they collect?
items.e: Add all three weeks. 18 + 24 = 42. Then 42 + 31 = 73 cans. (42, 55 and 49 add only two of the weeks.)

items.q: The school wanted 90 cans. They collected 73 cans. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: 90 − 73: count up from 73 to 80 (7), then 80 to 90 (10). 7 + 10 = 17 cans. (23 takes 0 from 3 the wrong way. 7 stops counting at 80.)

items.q: 18 students voted for a field trip. 9 chose the aquarium and 5 chose the science centre. The rest chose Stanley Park. How many chose Stanley Park?
items.e: 9 + 5 = 14 students chose the other places. 18 − 14 = 4 chose Stanley Park. (14 stops after adding. 13 only takes away 5.)

c: Relay race got the fewest votes.
The sack race is the fastest.
items.e: A pictograph shows how many chose each activity. The Relay race row is the shortest. It does not tell us why, or what is boring or fast.
